title: Exam Preparation at C1

pts: Study the exam's format, scoring criteria and underlying construct (what it claims to measure) before designing any preparation.
This connects directly to Unit 21's four test qualities — evaluate the target exam itself against validity and reliability standards.
Understanding the construct, not just the format, distinguishes genuine preparation from superficial format-drilling.

v: The official handbook or public sample materials for the target exam; the public band descriptors

items: Download the official handbook or sample materials for the target exam from the exam board’s website.
List each paper, its tasks, timing, number of items and weighting.
Read the published scoring criteria and write, in one sentence each, what ability every paper claims to measure.
Evaluate each paper against the four qualities from Unit 21: does it seem valid, reliable, practical, and likely to produce positive washback?
Compare two exams learners often choose between, such as IELTS Academic and C1 Advanced.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A construct note for one writing task (written for this book, based on the public IELTS writing criteria):

lines: Format: Academic Task 2, an essay of at least 250 words, about 40 minutes.
Criteria: Task Response; Coherence and Cohesion; Lexical Resource; Grammatical Range and Accuracy.
Construct in one sentence: the ability to develop and support a position in organized written academic English.
Implication: memorized introductions do little; argument-building does a great deal.

blocks.x: Formats and criteria are revised from time to time, so check the current handbook each year.

body: Purpose: to separate what the exam looks like from what it measures. Content: an iceberg; above the water, small labels ‘timing’, ‘question types’, ‘answer sheet’; below, a much larger mass labelled ‘reading academic texts’, ‘building an argument’, ‘listening to extended talk’, ‘interacting’. Style: clean, two colours. Board version: a triangle split by a wavy line with labels above and below.

items: Cambridge English and IELTS official websites (free) for handbooks, public sample papers and band descriptors [VERIFY current URLs and which materials are free].

blocks.x: A printed handbook and a one-page anatomy table in the teaching file.

points.h: Teaching the Exam vs. Teaching to the Exam
pts: 'Teaching the exam' builds genuine underlying competence the exam happens to measure; 'teaching to the exam' drills format-specific tricks divorced from real ability.
The washback principles from Unit 57 apply directly here — good exam preparation produces positive washback toward genuine skill.
Learners who only learn exam tricks often struggle with any communicative demand slightly outside the exam's specific format.

v: A list of ‘exam tips’ collected from coaching websites, books or learners

items: Learners list the exam tips they have heard (for example, ‘Always use a quotation in the introduction’).
In pairs, they sort each tip into ‘builds real ability’, ‘useful strategy’ or ‘trick’.
For each ‘trick’, pairs ask: would this help me in a real university seminar or office email?
Class discussion: which tips survive? What do the examiners’ criteria actually reward?
Agree a short class charter for the course (see model language).
Learners first discuss the tips in their home language, then report their decisions in English.
Support: give a ready list of ten tips to sort.
Challenge: learners check each tip against the public band descriptors.

lines: ‘Learn ten high-level words and use them in every essay.’ → trick; examiners reward appropriate vocabulary, not inserted vocabulary.
‘Skim the passage before reading the questions.’ → useful strategy; transfers to real reading.
‘Read widely on social and scientific topics.’ → builds real ability.

blocks.x: Class charter: We practise the exam format, but most of our time goes into reading, listening, writing and speaking for real.

body: Purpose: to contrast teaching the exam with teaching to the exam. Content: two paths up a hill to a flag marked ‘exam’; one narrow path ends at the flag; the other wider path continues past the flag to a university, an office and a hospital. Style: simple landscape. Board version: two lines to a flag, one continuing beyond it.

items: Padlet (free plan with limited boards) for collecting and sorting tips.

blocks.x: Tips on slips of paper sorted into three columns on the board.

pts: Learners do need genuine familiarity with an exam's format, timing and question types to perform at their real ability level.
Excessive time spent purely on format familiarisation, at the expense of underlying skill development, produces diminishing returns.
A reasonable balance dedicates most preparation time to genuine skill-building, with periodic, not constant, format practice.

v: The course calendar; the exam anatomy from point 1

items: Count the teaching hours available before the exam.
Allocate most of them to skill development, keeping a smaller share for format familiarization; a rough 80/20 split is a useful starting point, not a rule.
Place short format sessions at intervals, for example one per paper early on, then full mocks later.
Check that learners meet every paper’s format at least twice.
For a four-week course, shift the balance towards familiarization.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A twelve-week map, three hours a week (written for this book):

lines: Weeks 1–3: extensive reading and listening, argument building; one taster of each paper.
Weeks 4–8: skill blocks (academic writing, lecture listening, discussion); one timed paper every fortnight.
Weeks 9–11: two full mock exams with analysis; targeted skill work on the gaps.

blocks.x: The split is a teaching judgement. What matters is that familiarization is periodic, not constant.

body: Purpose: to show format practice as occasional windows in a skill-building course. Content: a twelve-week calendar strip, mostly green (‘skills’), with narrow orange windows (‘format’) that widen slightly near the end. Style: timeline infographic. Board version: a long bar with a few shaded sections.

items: Google Sheets (free) to plan and colour-code the calendar.

blocks.x: A calendar drawn on chart paper and pinned in the staff room.

pts: Time management, strategic skimming for exam reading tasks, and answer-elimination techniques are legitimate, genuinely transferable strategic skills.
This connects to Unit 27's strategic competence — exam strategy is one specific, high-value application of that broader competence.
Teach these explicitly rather than assuming learners will discover them through repeated practice alone.

v: One reading task from public sample material; a clock visible to all

items: Model a think-aloud: show how you skim the text in about two minutes, then read the questions.
Model answer elimination on one multiple-choice item, saying why each wrong option is wrong.
Learners try the same on the next three items in pairs, speaking their reasoning aloud.
Introduce a time plan for the whole paper and write it on the board.
Learners finish the task alone and compare how well they kept to the plan.
Apply the same sequence to a listening task.
Support: provide a written checklist of the three strategies.
Challenge: learners write a plausible distractor for a new item.

lines: T: Option A says ‘all scientists agree’. The text says ‘many researchers’. That’s too strong, so A goes. Option C is true, but it answers a different question. B and D are left. The writer says ‘however’ here, and then changes direction, so D.
Time plan (for a paper of about 90 minutes, written for this book): skim all texts 5 minutes; tasks in order of confidence; 10 minutes left to check.

blocks.x: These are forms of strategic competence (Unit 27): planning, monitoring and repair applied to a testing situation. Teaching them explicitly saves learners from having to discover them by trial and error.

body: Purpose: to summarize three teachable strategies. Content: three cards, a clock (‘plan your time’), an eye scanning lines (‘skim first’) and a crossed-out option (‘eliminate with a reason’). Style: flat icons, one line each. Board version: three boxes with a symbol and two words.

items: Classroomscreen (free version) for an on-screen timer.

blocks.x: A wall clock and the time plan written on the board.

body: Ask learners to justify every elimination aloud with a word or phrase from the text. This turns a guessing habit into careful reading, which is exactly what the reading paper claims to measure.

pts: High-stakes exams intensify the anxiety dynamics discussed in Unit 22, given their concentrated real-world consequences.
Realistic mock exam conditions, practised repeatedly, build the specific confidence a genuine exam situation demands.
Explicit strategy for managing in-exam anxiety (a paced breathing technique, a clear time-check routine) is worth direct teaching.

v: One full mock session plus 20 minutes preparation
A full practice test; exam-style seating; a printed routine card

items: Before the mock, teach a short routine: a slow breathing count, a time-check at set points, and a ‘stuck’ rule (mark it, move on, return).
Run the mock in realistic conditions: seating, timing, silence, instructions read aloud.
Afterwards, learners rate their anxiety at the start, middle and end (1–5).
Discuss which parts of the routine helped.
Repeat the mock later in the course and compare ratings.
For speaking, a colleague acts as examiner so that the face is unfamiliar.
Support: allow a first mock with a short break between papers.
Challenge: learners design their own personal routine card.

blocks.x: A routine card (written for this book):

lines: Before I start: breathe in for four, out for six, three times.
At each quarter of the time: check the clock and my plan.
If I’m stuck: circle it, move on, come back.

blocks.x: Foreign language anxiety is a well-documented factor in performance (Horwitz, Horwitz, and Cope 1986), and Unit 22 explored its classroom effects. Rehearsal reduces the novelty of the day itself.

body: Purpose: to make the routine memorable. Content: a learner at an exam desk with three small speech balloons: ‘breathe’, ‘check the clock’, ‘mark and move on’. Style: calm, pastel. Board version: three numbered lines.

items: Google Forms (free) for quick anxiety ratings.

blocks.x: Paper rating slips collected in an envelope.

pts: Use practice test results diagnostically — identifying specific skill gaps — rather than only as a general readiness check.
This connects to Unit 49's error-analysis principles, applied specifically to exam-task performance patterns.
A practice test that isn't analysed for specific gaps has only delivered half its potential value.

v: Marked practice test; an item-by-item results grid

items: After a practice test, enter every learner’s result for every item or task in a grid.
Group items by the skill they test (for example, inference, reference words, gist, word formation).
Calculate the class success rate for each skill group.
Learners complete their own error log (Unit 8) and look for patterns, as in Unit 49.
Plan the next two weeks around the two weakest skill groups.
For writing, analyse a set of scripts against each criterion instead of items.
Support: provide the skill labels for each item.
Challenge: learners write a short diagnostic report on themselves.

blocks.x: A class results summary (a fictional class):

lines: Gist questions: 78% correct · Reference words: 71% · Inference: 42% · Word formation: 55%

blocks.x: Decision: inference is the main gap. Next steps: reading lessons with ‘How do you know?’ questions; learners mark the words in the text that support each inference. A score says how much. An analysis says what next.

body: Purpose: to show diagnostic use of a practice test. Content: a single score of ‘58%’ on the left, an arrow to four skill bars of different lengths, and an arrow to a lesson plan labelled ‘inference’. Style: clear infographic. Board version: a number, four bars, a note.

items: Google Sheets or Microsoft Excel (free online version) for item analysis with a simple average formula.

blocks.x: A tally grid on paper and a hand-drawn bar chart.

body: Test developers routinely calculate how many candidates answer each item correctly, often called the item’s facility value (Hughes 2003). Teachers can use the same simple calculation on practice tests to see which skills a whole class finds hardest.

points.h: Balancing Exam Prep With Broader Development
pts: A course entirely focused on exam preparation, especially over an extended period, risks the narrow skill development Unit 47's plateau discussion warns against.
Where the timeline allows, integrate genuine Tier II and III methodology (task-based work, extensive input) alongside exam-specific preparation.
This produces a learner better prepared for both the specific exam and genuine post-exam language use.

v: 20 minutes a week across the course
Graded readers or authentic texts; a short weekly discussion task

items: Reserve a fixed weekly slot for non-exam English: extensive reading (Unit 31), a discussion, a short project.
Link it loosely to exam topics where possible (science, environment, work, education).
Learners keep a short reading or listening log.
Once a month, a small task-based project (Unit 28), such as a group report on a local issue.
A former student now studying abroad talks about the English they actually use.
Support: shorter, easier texts for extensive reading.
Challenge: learners present a podcast or article they chose themselves.

lines: T: Why read a newspaper feature six weeks before the exam?
S2: Because the exam has long texts. And after the exam we’ll read like this every day.

blocks.x: Unit 47 warns that long periods of narrow practice can lead to a plateau. A small, regular dose of extensive input keeps the whole language system growing.

body: Purpose: to contrast narrow and broad preparation. Content: a thin plant watered only by ‘past papers’ beside a bushy plant watered by ‘reading’, ‘talk’, ‘projects’ and ‘past papers’. Style: warm, simple. Board version: two stick plants.

items: BBC Learning English (free) for graded listening and news-based materials.

blocks.x: A class library box of newspapers, magazines and graded readers.

pts: Be honest with learners and institutions about realistic score expectations given a learner's actual starting level and available preparation time.
Avoid overselling guaranteed outcomes that depend on factors genuinely outside a teacher's control.
This connects to Unit 73's broader high-stakes-testing ethics discussion later in this tier.

v: Placement results; the course calendar; the exam’s band descriptors

items: Place each learner using a reliable placement task or a recent practice test.
Compare the learner’s current level with the target score and the time available.
Prepare a short, honest statement of what is realistic and what depends on the learner’s own work.
Hold the conversation with the learner (and, where appropriate, family or sponsoring institution).
Record the agreement and review it mid-course.
Draft an institutional policy that no advertising promises guaranteed scores.
Not applicable (teacher and learner discussion).

lines: A: My daughter needs a 7 in eight weeks. Can you guarantee it?

B: I can’t guarantee any score. Her last practice test was around 6. With regular work, a gain is possible, but eight weeks is short. I’ll show you her progress after each mock so that you can decide early whether to book a later date.

blocks.x: Honesty protects learners’ money and teachers’ integrity. Hamp-Lyons (1998) raised similar ethical questions about test-preparation materials. Unit 73 develops the wider ethics of high-stakes testing.

body: Purpose: to show expectations as a shared plan. Content: a line graph from ‘now’ to ‘exam date’ with a shaded band of possible outcomes rather than a single promised line; a teacher and learner look at it together. Style: calm. Board version: a line with a shaded band.

items: Google Docs (free) for a written expectations agreement.

blocks.x: A one-page printed agreement signed by the learner.

body: Take one exam class you teach now. Complete the exam anatomy in point 1, then check your last four weeks of lessons. What share went to real skill-building and what share to format practice? Change the balance for the next four weeks and compare the next practice-test profile.

dek: Unit 66 of 100: preparing learners for high-stakes exams like Cambridge C1 Advanced and IELTS effectively and ethically — teaching the exam without teaching only the exam.

aims.x: Sooner or later most teachers of advanced learners are asked to ‘prepare the class for the exam’. The exam may be Cambridge C1 Advanced, IELTS, a university entrance test or an employer’s screening test. This unit shows how to prepare learners for such exams in a way that raises their real ability as well as their scores, and how to do it honestly.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: analyse a target exam’s format, criteria and construct before planning a course;
distinguish teaching the abilities an exam measures from teaching narrow test tricks;
plan a realistic balance between format familiarization and skill development;
teach transferable exam strategies explicitly;
help learners manage anxiety through routines and realistic mock conditions;
use practice tests diagnostically to identify specific gaps;
keep broader language development alive during an exam course;
give learners and institutions honest, evidence-based expectations about scores.

why: Why this matters. Exam preparation is a genuine, common professional demand. Done well, it builds real ability; done poorly, it produces narrow test-passing skill that doesn't transfer.

background.x: High-stakes English exams shape lives in India. A band score can decide admission to a university abroad, a nursing registration, a visa or a job. Teachers therefore face strong pressure to ‘teach to the test’. At the same time, the major international exams claim to measure general academic or professional proficiency. If that claim is justified, the most efficient preparation is to build that proficiency.

Testing specialists describe the effect of a test on teaching and learning as washback (Alderson and Wall 1993). Samuel Messick (1996) argued that positive washback is more likely when a test directly samples the abilities it claims to measure, and that washback is best understood as one part of a test’s validity. Washback is not automatic: the same exam can lead one teacher to rich skill-building and another to endless past papers (Cheng, Watanabe, and Curtis 2004). Anthony Green’s (2007) study of IELTS writing preparation found that dedicated test-preparation courses did not produce clearly greater score gains than broader academic English courses [VERIFY exact findings and wording in Green 2007]. Unit 57 treats washback in depth, and Unit 73 returns to the ethics of high-stakes testing.

The four qualities introduced in Unit 21 (validity, reliability, practicality and washback) give teachers a way to evaluate the exam itself. The distinction that matters most here is between the format of a test, which is its paper, tasks and timing, and its construct, which is the ability it claims to measure (Bachman and Palmer 1996). Format can be learned in a few weeks. The construct takes much longer.

NEP 2020 calls for assessment that tests ‘core capacities’ rather than rote memorization and criticizes the coaching culture that high-stakes exams produce (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020). NCF 2023 makes a similar case for competency-based assessment (NCERT 2023). An ethical exam course in India respects both goals: it gets learners ready for a real exam they need, and it treats them as language users, not test-takers only. Discussing a strategy in Tamil or Malayalam can deepen understanding even when the exam itself is English only.

items: Exam anatomy. A one-page analysis of the target exam separating format from construct, with a judgement on its washback.
Course map. A calendar showing the balance of skill development and periodic format practice.
Diagnostic report. An item or criterion analysis of one practice test, with the resulting teaching plan.
Expectations record. A short written agreement with a learner, reviewed at the mid-point.
How much of your current exam course builds ability that will outlast the exam?
Which ‘exam tips’ do you pass on without checking them against the published criteria?
How do you use practice-test results beyond giving a score?
What do you say when a learner or parent asks you to guarantee a score?
How do you help learners manage anxiety on the day itself?

Green, A. 2007. IELTS Washback in Context: Preparation for Academic Writing in Higher Education. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.

perm: All tip lists, routine cards, dialogues, course maps and results tables are written for this book. Do not reproduce copyrighted exam papers, items or official handbooks; refer teachers to the exam boards’ public materials instead, and paraphrase band descriptors unless permission is obtained. Screenshots of exam-board websites, Padlet, Classroomscreen, Google Forms or Google Sheets require permission or replacement with original illustrations.

terms.def: An exam strategy in which learners rule out options they can show to be wrong before choosing an answer to a multiple-choice item; teachers model it by explaining why each wrong option fails.
The ability or quality a test aims to measure, such as reading comprehension or speaking fluency; a clear definition of the construct is the basis for valid assessment.

A transferable technique for doing well in a test, such as skimming questions before reading, managing time across sections or eliminating wrong options. It should support, not replace, development of the abilities the exam measures.
In item analysis, the proportion of test-takers who answer an item correctly, from 0 to 1. A value of 0.93 means almost everyone got it right, so the item tells the teacher little.
Making learners familiar with an exam’s format, question types and timing so that unfamiliarity does not lower their scores. It should take a smaller share of course time than skill development.
Analysing how each test item performed, using statistics such as facility value and discrimination index, to identify items that are too easy, too hard or faulty.
A practice examination under conditions similar to the real one, used to familiarize learners with format and timing and to identify areas that need more work.
Narrowing teaching to the content and formats of an examination, often at the expense of wider language skills. It is a common form of negative washback in high-stakes systems.

The structure and task types of a test, such as multiple choice, gap-fill, essay or oral interview, and their timing. Learners benefit from familiarity with a format, but this should not replace skill development.

The effect of a test on teaching and learning, which may be positive or negative (Alderson and Wall 1993). Board examinations that test only reading and writing often lead to neglect of listening and speaking.
